transcript.text: A tariff is a tax on imported goods that raises the domestic price above the world price. Domestic firms respond by producing more, consumers buy less, and imports fall. Consumers lose surplus, domestic producers gain surplus, and the government collects tariff revenue. The tariff also prevents mutually beneficial trades, creating deadweight loss from excessive domestic production and reduced consumption.
Begin with an importing country whose world price is below the domestic no-trade price.
Add the tariff per unit to the world price to find the tariff-inclusive domestic price.
At that higher price, read domestic quantity demanded and quantity supplied; imports equal their difference.
Tariff revenue equals the tariff per unit multiplied by the number of units imported.
Look for lower consumer surplus, higher producer surplus, government revenue, and deadweight loss from overproduction and underconsumption.
Do not treat tariff revenue as full welfare loss. Part of the consumer loss is transferred to producers and government; the production and consumption distortions are net losses.

The horizontal axis is quantity of phone cases and the vertical axis is their price in dollars. Quantity is measured in thousands as printed on the axis. Domestic demand slopes down and domestic supply slopes up, crossing at point e, price $8 and quantity 150 thousand. Horizontal lines mark world price $4 and domestic price with tariff $6. At $4, supply is 50 thousand and demand is 250 thousand; at $6, supply is 100 thousand and demand is 200 thousand.

At the $4 world price, domestic quantity demanded is 250 thousand and domestic quantity supplied is 50 thousand, so free-trade imports are 200 thousand. A $2 tariff raises the domestic price to $6; quantity demanded falls to 200 thousand and quantity supplied rises to 100 thousand. Imports fall to 100 thousand, and government tariff revenue is $2 x 100 thousand = $200 thousand.
Which two effects create tariff deadweight loss?
